questions.prompt: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?

options.text: They are the same thing
Authentication verifies who you are; authorization checks what you're allowed to do
Authentication checks permissions; authorization verifies identity
Authorization is only for admins

questions.explanation: Authentication establishes identity (who you are); authorization checks permissions (what you may do). You authenticate first, then authorize each action.

questions.prompt: How should user passwords be stored?

options.text: In plaintext for easy recovery
As a salted hash using a slow algorithm like bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2
Encrypted with a key stored next to them
As a fast unsalted MD5 hash

questions.explanation: A per-user salt defeats precomputed-hash attacks and a slow algorithm makes brute force expensive, so a database leak exposes hashes that are impractical to crack.

options.text: Encrypting data at rest
Delegated authorization — granting an app limited, scoped access to your data without sharing your password
Hashing passwords
Load balancing requests

questions.explanation: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework for delegated access: a user grants an app a scoped access token instead of their password. OpenID Connect adds authentication on top.

questions.prompt: An API authenticates users but fetches a record by id without checking ownership. What vulnerability is this?

options.text: A cache stampede
Broken access control — any logged-in user can access others' data by changing the id
A retry storm
A split brain

questions.explanation: Authentication is not authorization. Without a per-request ownership check, users can read others' records — broken access control, the most common serious web flaw.

questions.prompt: What is the principle of least privilege?

options.text: Give every service admin rights for convenience
Grant each user, service, and credential the minimum permissions needed and nothing more
Only the CEO gets access
Disable all permissions

questions.explanation: Least privilege limits each identity to the minimum access it needs, so a compromised component can do far less damage.

options.text: Yes, its contents are secret
No — a signed JWT is readable (base64) and only tamper-evident, so never put secrets in it
Yes, JWTs are always encrypted by default
Only if it contains a password

questions.explanation: A signed JWT proves integrity (it wasn't tampered with) but its payload is base64-encoded and readable. Don't store confidential data in one.
